# Case 4

57F, known AML, day 28 marrow after intensive induction. Morphological remission.

NGS at diagnosis:
- RUNX1 p.(Arg204Ter), VAF 44%
- SRSF2 p.(Pro95His), VAF 41%
- CSF3R p.(Thr618Ile), VAF 8%
- SETBP1 p.(Asp868Asn), VAF 7%

# NGS panel scope

This file defines the gene-level scope of the laboratory NGS panel used by this workflow.
It intentionally does not encode transcript, exon, or amplicon numbers.

## Negative-result semantics

When the patient NGS result is explicitly complete, a listed panel gene that is absent from the detected-variant list is interpreted as **no SNV, short insertion/deletion, or short-range complex variant detected in that gene within the validated assay scope**.

Use this negative result when applying diagnostic, prognostic, biomarker, treatment, germline, and other reporting rules. Do not treat the gene as unresolved merely because it is not individually listed in the patient result.

This inference is limited to the assay scope. It does not establish whole-gene biological wild type and does not exclude copy-number changes, rearrangements, structural variants, or other variant classes unless the patient result or another supplied test explicitly assesses them.

If the patient NGS result is described as partial, selected, limited, abbreviated, pending, or otherwise incomplete, do not infer a negative result for an unlisted panel gene.

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: Severe congenital neutropenia involving ELANE, CSF3R, GFI1, or SRP54 is listed as a germline predisposition associated with MDS and AML.
RUNX1 is listed as a germline predisposition gene associated with MDS and AML.
Poor stem-cell mobilization in a sibling candidate donor is reported as a rare clue to germline TERC or RUNX1 predisposition.
In MDS or AML, a RUNX1, GATA2, TP53, ETV6, or CEBPA variant detected on a somatic NGS panel with VAF 40–60% or >90% can suggest possible germline origin.

When a RUNX1, GATA2, TP53, ETV6, or CEBPA variant detected on a somatic NGS panel is suspected to be germline in MDS/AML, confirmation in extra-hematological tissue is highly recommended after consent.
Carriers of RUNX1, ANKRD26, or ETV6 variants may have thrombocytopenia at baseline.
Carriers of RUNX1, ANKRD26, or ETV6 variants may have a bleeding tendency even without thrombocytopenia.

In AML remission after intensive chemotherapy and before alloHCT, variants in germline-predisposition genes such as ANKRD26, CEBPA, DDX41, ETV6, GATA2, RUNX1 and TP53 are not prognostic for MRD and should not be counted toward MRD status at those time points.

AML classification is hierarchical: AML with a recurrent genetic abnormality takes precedence; among remaining categories, TP53-mutated disease supersedes myelodysplasia-related gene-mutated disease, which supersedes myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic disease.
For categories other than AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities, 10%-19% marrow or blood blasts are designated MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts are designated AML.
t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2)/PML::RARA defines APL/AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
t(8;21)(q22;q22.1)/RUNX1::RUNX1T1 defines AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
inv(16)(p13.1q22) or t(16;16)(p13.1;q22)/CBFB::MYH11 defines AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
t(9;11)(p21.3;q23.3)/MLLT3::KMT2A defines AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
t(6;9)(p22.3;q34.1)/DEK::NUP214 defines AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
inv(3)(q21.3q26.2) or t(3;3)(q21.3;q26.2)/GATA2,MECOM(EVI1) defines AML with at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.
Mutated NPM1 is an AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality when marrow or blood blasts are at least 10%.
An in-frame mutation in the CEBPA bZIP domain, monoallelic or biallelic, defines the CEBPA-mutated AML subtype when marrow or blood blasts are at least 10%.
AML with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)/BCR::ABL1 requires at least 20% marrow or blood blasts; cases with BCR::ABL1 rearrangement and 10%-19% blasts are classified as CML in accelerated phase.

In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), recurrent RARA rearrangements involving IRF2BP2, NPM1, ZBTB16, STAT5B, STAT3, TBL1XR1, FIP1L1, or BCOR should be reported as the specific RARA-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), recurrent KMT2A rearrangements with AFF1, AFDN, MLLT10, TET1, ELL, or MLLT1 should be reported as the specific KMT2A-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), recurrent MECOM rearrangements involving MYC, ETV6, RUNX1, or the listed t(2;3) MECOM rearrangement should be reported as the specific MECOM-rearranged entity; as AML-defining recurrent abnormalities, they apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the rare recurring rearrangements involving PRDM16::RPN1, RBM15::MRTFA, NPM1::MLF1, NUP98::NSD1, ETV6::MNX1, KAT6A::CREBBP, PICALM::MLLT10, NUP98::KMD5A or other NUP98 partners, FUS::ERG, RUNX1::CBFA2T3, and CBFA2T3::GLIS2 are AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormalities and apply at at least 10% marrow or blood blasts.

In the absence of an overriding AML-defining recurrent genetic abnormality, a pathogenic somatic TP53 mutation with VAF at least 10%, with or without loss of the wild-type TP53 allele, defines the TP53-mutated category; cases are MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts and AML at at least 20% blasts.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML) lacking an overriding recurrent AML abnormality and TP53 mutation, mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 define the myelodysplasia-related gene-mutated category irrespective of prior MDS; these cases are designated MDS/AML at 10%-19% blasts and AML at at least 20% blasts.

At least three unrelated chromosome abnormalities, excluding class-defining recurring abnormalities and hyperdiploid karyotypes with three or more trisomies/polysomies without structural abnormalities, is a complex karyotype sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

del(5q), t(5q), or add(5q) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

Monosomy 7 or del(7q) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.
Trisomy 8 is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

del(12p), t(12p), or add(12p) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.
i(17q) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

Monosomy 17, add(17p), or del(17p) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.
del(20q) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

idic(X)(q13) is sufficient for the myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic AML category when higher-priority categories are absent. In this branch, 10%-19% blasts is MDS/AML and at least 20% blasts is AML.

Remaining cases without a higher-priority AML-defining category are classified as AML, not otherwise specified, when blasts are at least 20%, irrespective of the presence or absence of multilineage dysplasia.
When a germline predisposing disorder is identified, it is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the specific genetically defined AML disease category rather than replacing that primary category.

In germline CEBPA-mutation carriers, distinct acquired CEBPA mutations can re-emerge as independent primary AMLs rather than representing relapse, so recurrence may require distinction between a new primary AML and relapse.
Prior cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immune intervention for a nonmyeloid neoplasm is recorded as a therapy-related diagnostic qualifier rather than defining a separate AML disease entity.
Progression from MDS is appended as a diagnostic qualifier when the antecedent MDS was confirmed by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis.
Multiparameter flow-cytometric immunophenotyping is required to diagnose AML accurately by identifying cell-surface and intracellular markers.
In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), when bone-marrow aspirate is unobtainable and circulating blasts are absent, myeloid phenotype may be confirmed on a core biopsy by immunohistochemistry.
Conventional cytogenetic analysis is mandatory in the evaluation of AML.

In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), if conventional cytogenetics yields no analyzable metaphases, FISH is an alternative for detecting specified recurrent fusions and myelodysplasia-related chromosome abnormalities.
Myeloblasts, monoblasts, and megakaryoblasts are included in the marrow or blood blast count used for AML classification.
In AML with monocytic or myelomonocytic differentiation, monoblasts and promonocytes are counted as blast equivalents, whereas abnormal monocytes are not.
In AML with PML::RARA or a variant RARA rearrangement, promyelocytes are counted as blast equivalents for classification.
Remaining cases without a higher-priority AML-defining category are designated MDS/AML otherwise not specified when marrow or blood blasts are 10%-19%.
Table 2 identifies RUNX1 as a gene associated with germline predisposition due to RUNX1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants, with lifelong thrombocytopenia/qualitative platelet defects.
In germline RUNX1 predisposition, about 30% of patients have clonal hematopoiesis before leukemia development, with BCOR mutations predominating in that clonal hematopoiesis.
Among the RUNX1, ANKRD26, and ETV6 platelet-disorder predisposition syndromes, germline ANKRD26 mutation carriers generally have the lowest platelet counts.
Germline RUNX1 mutations predispose to myeloid malignancies, T-cell ALL, and B-cell malignancies.
When leukemia develops in germline RUNX1 predisposition, somatic mutation of the wild-type RUNX1 allele is common, together with acquired mutations in ASXL1, FLT3, GATA2, PHF6, SRSF2, and WT1.
Do not apply the 2024 ELN Less-Intensive classification to AML patients who have received prior HMA treatment.
In CMML, JAK2, NRAS, and SETBP1 mutations were significantly associated with the myeloproliferative subtype (CMML-MP).
WHO5 retains a 20% blast cutoff to delineate MDS from AML while removing blast cutoffs for most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities.
WHO5 recognizes AML with PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1 and CBFB::MYH11 as AML types with defining genetic abnormalities.
AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation are the defining-genetic-abnormality AML types that still require at least 20% blasts; for BCR::ABL1 this avoids overlap with CML.
AML with KMT2A, MECOM or NUP98 rearrangement may be diagnosed with a blast count below 20%.
AML with NPM1 mutation can be diagnosed irrespective of blast count, with clinicopathologic correlation.
AML with CEBPA mutation includes biallelic CEBPA mutations and single CEBPA mutations in the basic leucine zipper region.
Somatic RUNX1 mutation is not sufficient to define a standalone WHO5 AML type because it lacks specificity across defining molecular contexts.
AML, myelodysplasia-related has a mutation-based definition that includes SRSF2, SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, ASXL1, EZH2, BCOR or STAG2.
Morphologic myelodysplasia alone is no longer sufficient to diagnose AML, myelodysplasia-related.
In acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia, the RAM immunophenotype correlates with CBFA2T3::GLIS2, a subtype of AML with other defined genetic alterations.

For many RUNX1 variants detected on tumor-based sequencing, variant identity alone cannot establish constitutional status because the same variant may be somatic or germline; suspected germline status should be confirmed using true germline DNA.

For familial MDS/AML germline assessment, this review lists ANKRD26, CEBPA, DDX41, ETV6, GATA2, MBD4, MECOM/EVI1, PTPN11, RUNX1, SAMD9, SAMD9L, SRP72, and TET2 among genes recommended as yielding clinically actionable results.

In patients investigated for unexplained cytopenia, a negative result across the studied 40-gene panel did not exclude the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML): the negative predictive value was 0.76, increasing to 0.84 when mutation status was combined with standard karyotyping.

In patients investigated for unexplained cytopenia, finding two or more somatic mutations in the studied 40-gene panel was strongly predictive of the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML), with positive predictive value 0.88 (95% CI 0.84-0.92). These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

For mutations measured in isolated peripheral-blood granulocytes, a VAF around 0.10 was associated with the best classification of the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML); the paper cautions that the applicable allele-burden threshold may vary when a different blood-cell source is used. These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

In unexplained cytopenia, mutations in SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, JAK2, or RUNX1 had the highest predictive values for the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML), with positive predictive values of 0.88-0.97 irrespective of co-occurring mutations. These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

In unexplained cytopenia, isolated TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 mutations were substantially less predictive of the study's composite myeloid-neoplasm endpoint (MDS, MDS/MPN, MPN, or AML) than the same mutations occurring with additional genetic lesions (positive predictive value 0.29-0.57 vs 0.81-0.89). These predictive findings were reported as fully confirmed in the independent 190-patient validation cohort.

Primary myelofibrosis with JAK2 co-mutation was the stated specificity exception for SRSF2 or U2AF1: after excluding this pattern, SRSF2 and U2AF1 mutations showed 100% specificity for myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia.

In cases with inconclusive dysplasia, highly specific mutation patterns may provide presumptive evidence of MDS even without definitive morphology. The reported patterns included splicing-factor mutations and co-mutation patterns involving TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, or IDH1/IDH2; SRSF2/U2AF1 with JAK2 in primary myelofibrosis was a stated specificity exception.
